Glenn Curtiss. The aviation pioneer who competed with the Wright Brothers for dominance in early aviation. In 1909, Curtiss set a world speed record of forty-six and a half miles per hour. He designed the Pusher biplane with innovative wing-warping control, directly competing with the Wrights' design. That year he won the Gordon Bennett Cup, a prestigious international aviation race. Curtiss founded the Curtiss Aeroplane Company, one of the first successful aircraft manufacturers in America. His career was defined by decades of patent litigation with the Wright Brothers over aircraft control mechanisms. He developed the hydrofoil and amphibious aircraft, expanding aviation's scope beyond land-based flight. Curtiss designed the Curtiss Jenny, which became the primary trainer aircraft for American pilots during World War One. The aircraft that Charles Lindbergh later flew descended from innovations Curtiss pioneered. Though his legal disputes with the Wright Brothers dominated his legacy, he proved himself a talented engineer and successful industrialist.
